q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, the compound responsible for the smell of rancid butter?
h: Count every carbon, including the –COOH carbon, and use the ending “-oic acid.”
w: Four carbons including the carboxyl carbon: butanoic acid (butyric acid). Forgetting to count the COOH carbon gives propanoic acid.

q: Ethyl acetate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is a solvent in nail-polish remover. What is its IUPAC name?
h: The alkyl group on the single-bonded O is named first; the part containing C=O becomes “-oate.”
w: The acid part is CH3CO– (ethanoate) and the alcohol part is ethyl: ethyl ethanoate. Methyl propanoate is an isomer, CH3CH2COOCH3.

q: Propanoic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the organic product?
h: Esterification: the –OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol leave as water.
w: CH3CH2COOH + HOCH3 → CH3CH2COOCH3 (methyl propanoate) + H2O. Ethyl ethanoate has the same formula but comes from acetic acid and ethanol.

q: Which species are present in an aqueous solution of acetic acid (vinegar), besides water and CH<sub>3</sub>COOH molecules?
h: A carboxylic acid is a weak acid. Which H does it donate to water?
w: The –COOH donates its H to water: CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO− + H3O+. Only a small fraction ionizes, so most of the acid stays as molecules.

q: What are the products of the neutralization of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide?
h: Acid + base → salt + water. Which ion replaces the acidic H?
w: CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COO−Na+ (sodium ethanoate, sodium acetate) + H2O. The carbon count of the acid does not change, so it is not a methanoate.

q: Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative instead of benzoic acid mainly because sodium benzoate
c: is ionic and more soluble in water
is a stronger acid than benzoic acid
has a higher molar mass than benzoic acid
is nonpolar and dissolves in fats
h: Compare a neutral carboxylic acid with its carboxylate salt.
w: Carboxylate salts are ionic, so they dissolve far better in water than the acids, which have a large nonpolar ring. The same idea is used to make many drugs water-soluble.

q: Propyl ethanoate (the odor of pears) is hydrolyzed in acid. What are the products?
h: Hydrolysis reverses esterification. The “-oate” part becomes the acid; the alkyl part becomes the alcohol.
w: CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 + H2O → CH3COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH3CH2CH2OH (1-propanol). Swapping the parts gives propanoic acid and ethanol, the hydrolysis products of a different ester.

q: Methyl butanoate is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: In base, the carboxylic acid formed is neutralized immediately.
w: Base hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt, sodium butanoate, and the alcohol, methanol. The free acid forms only in acid hydrolysis or after acidifying.

q: These compounds all have molar mass 74 g mol⁻¹. Which has the highest boiling point?
h: Count the hydrogen-bonding sites. Carboxylic acids can pair up through two hydrogen bonds.
w: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H bonds per pair), so propanoic acid (141 °C) boils above 1-butanol (118 °C). Esters and ethers have no O–H and boil much lower.

q: Aspirin, acetylsalicylic acid, contains which two functional groups?
c: a carboxylic acid and an ester
h: Aspirin is made by acetylating the phenol –OH of salicylic acid; the –COOH stays.
w: The original –COOH remains, and the phenol –OH becomes an acetyl ester, so aspirin has a carboxylic acid and an ester. Salicylic acid itself has the phenol group.

q: Lactic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)COOH, is a carboxylic acid (a weak acid). In blood at pH 7.4, lactic acid exists mainly as
h: At body pH, does a carboxylic acid keep its H<sup>+</sup> or lose it?
w: Carboxylic acids are weak acids that give up their H+ at body pH (7.4), so lactic acid is present as the carboxylate ion, lactate. That is why we say “lactate” in physiology.

q: This ester has a fruity smell: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Choose its correct name.
h: Split the ester at the single C–O next to C=O. The O–alkyl side is named first (-yl); the C=O side ends in -oate.
w: The C=O side, CH3CH2CO–, has 3 carbons (propanoate); the alkyl on the O, –CH2CH2CH3, is propyl: propyl propanoate. "Ethyl butanoate" comes from splitting on the wrong side of the C=O carbon.

q: Butanoic acid reacts with ethanol (H<sup>+</sup>, heat) to make ethyl butanoate, which smells like pineapple. Which is the ester?
h: The double-bond O side comes from the acid (4 carbons); the O–alkyl side comes from the alcohol (2 carbons).
w: Esterification removes –OH from the acid and H from the alcohol (lost as H2O): CH3CH2CH2CO– + –OCH2CH3 = CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3. CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 is an isomer (propyl propanoate) with the carbons split the wrong way.

q: Isopentyl acetate, CH<sub>3</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, gives bananas their smell. Which acid and alcohol are used to make it?
h: The C=O side came from the carboxylic acid; the group on the single-bonded O came from the alcohol.
w: CH3CO– is the acetate (acetic acid) part. The O–alkyl group –CH2CH2CH(CH3)2 came from HOCH2CH2CH(CH3)2, 3-methyl-1-butanol: acetic acid and 3-methyl-1-butanol.

q: Isobutyl formate, HCOOCH<sub>2</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, adds a raspberry-like note to flavorings. If this ester undergoes acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, which products form?
h: Acid hydrolysis cuts the single C–O bond next to the C=O; the C=O side becomes a carboxylic acid.
w: Breaking the C–O bond gives HCOOH (the C=O side) and HOCH2CH(CH3)2 (the O–alkyl side): methanoic acid and 2-methyl-1-propanol. Swapping the sides gives 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol; a carboxylate salt only forms in base (NaOH), not in acid.

q: Saponification of ethyl propanoate, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, with NaOH yields which two products?
h: In base hydrolysis (saponification), the acid part comes out as a salt. Which side of the ester is the acid part?
w: Saponification splits the ester at the C–O next to the C=O. The C=O side becomes the carboxylate salt CH3CH2COO−Na+ and the O–alkyl side becomes CH3CH2OH: sodium propanoate and ethanol. Propanoic acid itself would be the acid-hydrolysis product.

q: Isocaproic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH, has an unpleasant cheesy odor. Which IUPAC name is correct for this acid?
h: The –COOH carbon is C1. Count along the longest chain from it to the branch.
w: The carboxyl carbon is C1; the chain has 5 carbons and the CH3 is on C4: 4-methylpentanoic acid. Counting the branch carbon into the chain (hexanoic) or numbering from the other end (2-methyl) are the usual slips; "-al" would mean an aldehyde.

q: Butanoic acid, which gives rancid butter its odor, reacts with sodium hydroxide as shown below. Which term best describes this reaction?
h: Butanoic acid is a carboxylic acid and NaOH is a base. What happens when an acid meets a base?
w: The base removes the acidic H from –COOH to make a carboxylate salt (sodium butanoate) and water: neutralization. Saponification also uses NaOH, but its reactant is an ester, not an acid.

q: After it is swallowed, aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is hydrolyzed at its ester group by enzymes in the body. Which two products form?
h: Find aspirin's ester group. Its C=O side is an acetyl group (2 carbons); its O side is attached to the ring.
w: Aspirin's ester is Ar–O–CO–CH3. Hydrolysis breaks that C–O bond: the C=O side becomes acetic acid and the O side becomes the phenol –OH of salicylic acid: salicylic acid and acetic acid. Methanol would come from methyl salicylate, a different ester.

q: An ester is written as CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of it produces which pair?
h: Do not just read left to right. Find the C=O carbon: that side becomes the acid.
w: The C=O carbon is bonded to –CH2CH3, so the acid part is CH3CH2COOH (3 C); the –OCH3 becomes methanol. This is methyl propanoate, so the products are propanoic acid and methanol. Acetic acid and ethanol would come from its isomer ethyl ethanoate.

q: Acetic acid and isoamyl alcohol react with an acid catalyst (H<sup>+</sup>) to make isoamyl acetate, which smells like bananas. Which structure is the ester formed?
h: The C=O side of the ester comes from the acid; the alcohol supplies the –O–R part. Water is lost.
w: The –OH from the acid and the H from the alcohol leave as H2O, joining CH3C(=O)– to –O–CH2CH2CH(CH3)2: isoamyl acetate. The first wrong ester puts the C=O on the alcohol side (ethyl 3-methylbutanoate); the ether has lost the C=O; the last one attaches the O to the wrong carbon of the alcohol.

q: Salicylic acid reacts with methanol in acid to make methyl salicylate (oil of wintergreen, used in muscle rubs). Which structure is the product?
h: Esterification joins a carboxylic acid (–COOH) and an alcohol. Which group of salicylic acid is the acid?
w: Methanol reacts with the –COOH group, giving the methyl ester –COOCH3; the phenol –OH is unchanged. Methylating the phenol O gives an ether, not the ester. The structure with an acetyl group is aspirin, made with acetic acid, not methanol.

q: Ethyl butanoate (pineapple flavor), shown, is heated with water and an acid catalyst. What are the products?
h: Acid hydrolysis splits the ester at the C–O single bond next to the C=O and adds H and OH.
w: The ester bond between the carbonyl carbon and the –O– breaks; OH goes to the acyl group and H to the oxygen: butanoic acid + ethanol. Butanol + acetic acid splits the molecule at the wrong place; the sodium salt forms only in base (NaOH); two alcohols would require reduction.

q: Ethyl propanoate, shown, is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
h: In base, the carboxylic acid that forms is immediately neutralized. Which fragment carries the C=O?
w: NaOH breaks the C–O bond next to the C=O; the acyl part becomes the carboxylate salt and the –OCH2CH3 part becomes ethanol: sodium propanoate + ethanol. Propanoic acid + ethanol are the acid-hydrolysis products; the other choices put the Na+ or the C=O on the wrong fragment.

q: Methyl benzoate, shown, is saponified with NaOH. One product, sodium benzoate, is used as a food preservative. What are the products?
h: Saponification gives the alcohol and the salt of the carboxylic acid. The C=O stays with the acid part.
w: The ester splits at the C–O bond next to the C=O: the benzoyl part becomes sodium benzoate and the –OCH3 part becomes methanol. Benzoic acid + methanol form in acid, not base; the last choice puts the C=O on the wrong side of the ester oxygen (acetate + phenol).

q: The ester shown is a solvent with a fruity odor used in some nail-polish removers. What is its name?
h: Name the alkyl group on the –O– first, then the acid part (the side with the C=O) as "-oate".
w: The –O– carries an isopropyl group (attached at its middle carbon), and the C=O side has 2 carbons (ethanoate, from ethanoic/acetic acid): isopropyl ethanoate (isopropyl acetate). Propyl has the O on an end carbon; ethyl 2-methylpropanoate swaps the two sides; propanoate has 3 carbons on the C=O side.

q: Benzoic acid is used to preserve liquid medicines and sodas. Which form shown is the most soluble in water?
h: An ionic compound dissolves by ion–dipole attractions, which are stronger than hydrogen bonds to one –COOH group.
w: Sodium benzoate is an ionic salt: the Na+ and the –COO− group are each surrounded by water molecules, so it dissolves very well (over 500 g L⁻¹). That is why preservatives are added as the salt. Benzoic acid itself dissolves only about 3 g L⁻¹ because its benzene ring is nonpolar; chlorobenzene and toluene (about 0.5 g L⁻¹ each) cannot hydrogen bond with water at all.

q: What is the organic product of the reaction of benzoic acid and ethanol shown?
h: Esterification: the acid loses –OH, the alcohol loses H, and the acid C=O carbon bonds to the alcohol O.
w: The C=O carbon of benzoic acid bonds to the O of ethanol, and H2O is lost: ethyl benzoate. Benzyl acetate has the same formula but puts the C=O on the ethanol side. The ether has lost the C=O oxygen, and the ketone joins carbon to carbon instead of through oxygen.

q: Which ester forms in the reaction of 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol shown?
h: The acid keeps all its branches and its C=O. Swap its –OH for –O–CH<sub>3</sub> from methanol.
w: The branched acid becomes the "-oate" part and methanol supplies –OCH3: methyl 2-methylpropanoate + H2O. Isopropyl acetate is an isomer with the C=O on the wrong side of the ester oxygen. The ether has no C=O, and the ketone joins the CH3 directly to carbon.

q: Benzyl acetate, shown, gives jasmine its scent. Which carboxylic acid and alcohol react (H<sup>+</sup>, heat) to make it?
h: Split the ester at the single C–O bond next to the C=O. The C=O side was the acid; the other side was the alcohol.
w: The C=O side is CH3C(=O)– (from acetic acid) and the –O–CH2–C6H5 side is from benzyl alcohol. Benzoic acid + ethanol puts the C=O on the ring side (ethyl benzoate), and phenylacetic acid + methanol gives methyl phenylacetate; both are isomers. Acetic acid + phenol gives phenyl acetate, which is missing the CH2.

q: Butyl acetate is a solvent with a pear-like odor. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Break the single C–O bond next to the C=O. Add OH to the carbonyl carbon and H to the other O.
w: Water splits the ester into the acid part and the alcohol part: acetic acid + 1-butanol. Butanoic acid + ethanol breaks the molecule on the wrong side of the oxygen. Sodium acetate only forms in base (saponification), and two alcohols would require reduction.

q: What are the products of the saponification of ethyl 2-methylpropanoate shown?
h: Same split as acid hydrolysis, but in base the acid part comes out as its sodium salt (–COO<sup>−</sup> Na<sup>+</sup>).
w: NaOH breaks the C–O bond next to the C=O: the acid part becomes sodium 2-methylpropanoate and the –OCH2CH3 part becomes ethanol. The neutral acid + ethanol are the products in acid, not base. Putting Na+ on the ethanol O, or the C=O on the two-carbon piece, splits the ester wrongly.

q: Lactic acid builds up in hard-working muscle. What is the organic product of the neutralization shown?
h: Only the acidic H of –COOH reacts with a base. Everything else stays the same.
w: OH− removes the H from the –COOH group, giving sodium lactate (used in lactated Ringer's IV solution) + H2O. The alcohol –OH is far less acidic and is not deprotonated by NaOH. Sodium pyruvate would require oxidation of the alcohol, and the C=C product would require dehydration.

q: Hexanoic acid gives goats their strong odor. In the reaction shown, bubbles of CO<sub>2</sub> form. What is the organic product?
h: Carboxylic acids are strong enough to react with bicarbonate. Where do the CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O come from?
w: HCO−3 removes the acidic H, giving sodium hexanoate, and the H2CO3 formed breaks down to CO2 + H2O. The CO2 comes from the bicarbonate, not from the acid, so pentane is wrong. Hexanol would need reduction, and "no reaction" ignores that the bubbling shows a reaction.

q: An ester is heated with NaOH. The products are sodium butanoate and 2-propanol, shown. Which ester was used?
h: Rejoin the pieces: the carboxylate C=O carbon bonds to the O of the alcohol.
w: Joining the butanoyl group to the O of 2-propanol gives isopropyl butanoate. Propyl butanoate would give 1-propanol (O on the end carbon). Propyl 2-methylpropanoate puts the isopropyl group on the C=O side. The ether has no C=O and is not saponified.

q: Which reagent carries out the conversion shown (heating is used)?
h: The product side shows a carboxylate salt with Na<sup>+</sup>. Which reaction makes a salt instead of a carboxylic acid?
w: Saponification with NaOH splits the ester into sodium pentanoate and methanol. H2O/H+ also splits the ester but gives neutral pentanoic acid, not the sodium salt. H2/Ni does not reduce an ester C=O, and K2Cr2O7 oxidizes alcohols, not esters.

q: Formic acid and ethanol react as shown to make an ester with a rum-like odor. Which structure is the ester?
h: Formic acid supplies H–C(=O)–; ethanol supplies –O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>.
w: The formyl carbon bonds to the ethanol oxygen and water is lost: ethyl formate (ethyl methanoate), H–C(=O)–O–CH2CH3. Methyl acetate and propanoic acid have the same formula, C3H6O2, but the carbons are arranged differently. Ethyl methyl ether has no C=O.

q: Methyl salicylate is the active ingredient in wintergreen muscle rubs. What are the products of the reaction shown?
h: Find the ester group (C=O bonded to O–CH<sub>3</sub>). Only that bond is hydrolyzed; the ring –OH stays.
w: Water splits the –C(=O)–O–CH3 bond, giving salicylic acid + methanol. The sodium salt only forms with NaOH. Turning the C=O into CH2OH would be reduction. Salicylic acid + acetic acid are the hydrolysis products of aspirin, a different ester.

q: The acetate ion forms when acetic acid (vinegar) loses H<sup>+</sup>. One Lewis structure is drawn below. How many equivalent resonance structures does the acetate ion have?
h: Only the –COO<sup>−</sup> part has electrons that can move. Which atoms could share the C=O double bond?
w: The C=O double bond and the −1 charge can be on either oxygen, giving 2 equivalent structures. The CH3 carbon has no lone pairs or double bonds to move, so it adds none.

q: Sodium benzoate, a food preservative, contains the benzoate ion drawn below. In the real ion, the two carbon–oxygen bonds of the –COO<sup>−</sup> group are the same length. Why?
c: Resonance spreads the double bond and − charge over both O atoms.
Both oxygens form single bonds and each carries a full − charge.
The two oxygens rapidly pass an H<sup>+</sup> back and forth between them.
Both bonds are full C=O double bonds, so neither O is charged.
h: Draw a second structure that moves only electrons. Where can the double bond go?
w: The double bond can be drawn to either oxygen, so the real ion is an average of two equivalent structures: each C–O bond is between single and double, and the − charge is spread over both oxygens. Benzoate has no H on oxygen to trade, and it has only one negative charge.

q: The drawn compound is a beta-amino acid used to make some drugs. Name it by IUPAC rules.
h: The –COOH carbon is C1. Number toward the NH<sub>2</sub> and name it as an "amino" prefix.
w: The carboxylic acid carbon is C1, so the chain is numbered from it: C2 is the CH2, and the NH2 is on C3, giving 3-aminobutanoic acid. 4-Aminobutanoic acid (GABA) would have the NH2 on the last carbon; "butanal" would require an aldehyde instead of the acid.

q: When each drawn compound is dissolved in water, only one releases H<sup>+</sup> and lowers the pH. Which is that organic acid?
h: Of the common oxygen- and nitrogen-containing groups, only one donates a proton to water.
w: The –COOH group of butanoic acid loses its O–H proton to water (CH3CH2CH2COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3CH2CH2COO− + H3O+). Butylamine is a base (it accepts H+). The alcohol has an O–H, but it is essentially neutral in water; the aldehyde has no acidic H at all.

q: An ester is hydrolyzed once with aqueous acid and once with aqueous NaOH. How do the organic products differ?
c: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid; base hydrolysis gives its carboxylate salt. The alcohol released is the same.
Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt; base hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid. The alcohol released is the same.
Acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol; base hydrolysis gives an aldehyde instead.
The products are identical; only the reaction rate differs.
h: In base, any carboxylic acid that forms is immediately neutralized by the OH<sup>−</sup> present.
w: Both reactions cut the ester at the C–O single bond, releasing the alcohol. In acid the carbonyl piece is the free carboxylic acid; in NaOH the acid is neutralized to the sodium carboxylate salt (saponification). No aldehyde forms in either case, and the products are not identical because the salt is ionic.

q: Methyl butanoate smells like apples. Which drawing matches this ester name?
h: In an ester name, the first word is the alkyl group on the single-bonded O; the "-oate" part contains the C=O.
w: "Butanoate" means a four-carbon chain that includes the C=O carbon, and "methyl" is the one-carbon group on the other oxygen: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>C(=O)–O–CH<sub>3</sub>. Butyl methanoate has the same formula but the groups swapped (the C=O is in the one-carbon part). Methyl propanoate has one carbon too few in the acid part; ethyl propanoate puts two carbons on the oxygen.

q: Ant stings contain HCOOH. What is its IUPAC name?
h: Count the carbons: one carbon, and the –COOH group is the acid ending.
w: One carbon with a carboxyl group: methanoic acid (common name formic acid). Methanol is an alcohol and methanal an aldehyde.

q: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH?
h: Count every carbon, including the one in –COOH.
w: Three carbons, the COOH carbon is C1: propanoic acid.

q: Which carboxylic acid is the most soluble in water?
h: The COOH group hydrogen bonds with water; what does a long hydrocarbon tail do?
w: Small acids (up to about 4 carbons) mix with water; each extra CH2 adds nonpolar surface, so ethanoic acid is the most soluble.

q: Acetic acid (60 g mol⁻¹) boils at 118 °C, higher than 1-propanol (60 g mol⁻¹, 97 °C). Why?
c: two acetic acid molecules hydrogen bond to each other twice, forming dimers
acetic acid is an ionic compound
acetic acid has more dispersion forces because it has more carbons
h: Both can hydrogen bond. How many hydrogen bonds can a pair of acid molecules make?
w: Carboxylic acids pair up into hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H bonds per pair), so they boil higher than alcohols of similar molar mass.

q: Esters boil at much lower temperatures than carboxylic acids of similar molar mass because esters
c: have no O–H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond to one another
h: Look for an H bonded to O in an ester.
w: An ester has C=O and C–O–C but no O–H, so ester molecules attract each other only by dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

q: Which compound is the strongest acid?
h: Rank: alcohol, phenol, carboxylic acid.
w: Acid strength: carboxylic acid > phenol > water ≈ alcohol. The carboxylate ion is stabilized because its negative charge is shared by two oxygens.

q: What is the name of CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>?
h: Name a carboxylate salt like any salt: metal first, then the anion with an -ate ending.
w: The metal is named first, and the acid ending -ic acid becomes -ate: sodium acetate (IUPAC: sodium ethanoate).

q: 1-Butanol is heated with excess K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>. Which carboxylic acid forms?
h: Oxidation does not change the number of carbons; excess oxidizing agent goes past the aldehyde.
w: A primary alcohol with excess oxidizing agent goes alcohol → aldehyde → butanoic acid, keeping all four carbons.

q: Glucose 6-phosphate, the first product of glycolysis, is an ester of phosphoric acid and
h: A phosphate ester is made the same way as a carboxylic ester: acid + ?
w: Phosphoric acid condenses with the –OH on carbon 6 of glucose, losing water, to make a phosphate ester.
